content: Lichen sclerosus is a chronic inflammatory skin disorder that predominantly affects the genital and perianal regions. It is most commonly observed in adult women but can also occur in men and children. The condition is characterized by persistent itching and soreness in the affected areas. If left untreated, the inflammation can lead to scarring, which may result in significant anatomical changes. In women and girls, this can include fusion of the labia, narrowing of the vaginal opening, and burial of the clitoris. In men and boys, it can cause tightening of the foreskin. Additionally, individuals with lichen sclerosus are at an increased risk of developing genital cancers. The purpose of this study was to evaluate the effectiveness and adverse effects of topical treatments for genital lichen sclerosus. A comprehensive search of multiple databases was conducted up to September 16, 2011, to identify relevant randomized controlled trials (RCTs). Seven RCTs involving 249 participants were included in the analysis, covering six different treatments. One trial demonstrated that clobetasol propionate 0.05% was effective in treating genital lichen sclerosus. Participants reported significant improvement or remission of symptoms (risk ratio 2.85, 95% confidence interval 1.45 to 5.61), and investigators noted a marked global improvement (standardized mean difference 5.74, 95% confidence interval 4.26 to 7.23) compared to placebo. Another trial showed that mometasone furoate 0.05% significantly improved the clinical grade of phimosis (standardized mean difference -1.04, 95% confidence interval -1.77 to -0.31) compared to placebo. Importantly, neither trial reported significant differences in adverse drug reactions between the corticosteroid and placebo groups. Four trials evaluated the use of topical testosterone, dihydrotestosterone, and progesterone, but no significant benefits were observed. In fact, one trial found that topical testosterone, when used as maintenance therapy following initial treatment with clobetasol propionate, worsened symptoms (P < 0.05), whereas placebo did not. A separate trial compared pimecrolimus to clobetasol propionate. While there were no significant differences between the two treatments in terms of reducing itching (standardized mean difference -0.33, 95% confidence interval -0.99 to 0.33) or burning/pain (standardized mean difference 0.03, 95% confidence interval -0.62 to 0.69), pimecrolimus was less effective than clobetasol propionate in achieving global improvement as rated by investigators (standardized mean difference -1.64, 95% confidence interval -2.40 to -0.87). No significant differences in adverse drug reactions were reported between pimecrolimus and placebo groups. In conclusion, the available evidence supports the efficacy of clobetasol propionate, mometasone furoate, and pimecrolimus in the treatment of genital lichen sclerosus. However, further randomized controlled trials are necessary to determine the optimal potency and regimen of topical corticosteroids, explore other topical treatments, assess the duration of remission or prevention of disease flares, evaluate the potential reduction in the risk of genital squamous cell carcinoma or intraepithelial neoplasia, and investigate the impact of these treatments on the quality of sexual life in affected individuals.
